items.title: Drones knock out a third Yandex data center in a week
items.summary: On Sunday, Yandex said operations at its Vladimir data center were "completely suspended" after a drone attack, and its platform was running in emergency mode. The Sasovo hub was hit on Thursday; it houses two of the three supercomputers Yandex uses to build its AI models. Kaluga was partly knocked out on Friday.
items.why: AI data centers are now military targets, so physical security and geographic redundancy are becoming part of what compute actually costs.

items.title: Senate report: big data center builders won't commit to paying for grid upgrades
items.summary: Sens. Warren, Blumenthal and Van Hollen investigated Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, CoreWeave, Digital Realty and Equinix. None would accept a standard requiring them to pay for new power infrastructure their sites make necessary. The companies that shared jobs data reported about one permanent worker per megawatt, and the report estimates GPUs make up about 39% of spending at a 1 GW site (Time). Meanwhile, the bipartisan "Four Corners" permitting bill (BAAJA) would speed approvals for power lines, solar and pipelines serving AI demand. It needs 60 votes, and a vote before the Nov. 3 midterm
items.why: The 25→70 GW build-out depends on two political questions: who pays for the grid, and how fast permits clear.
items.source: Office of Sen. Warren · Time · Fortune

items.title: WSJ: Anthropic's compute hunt went through Meta (who said no) and SpaceX ($1.25B a month)
items.summary: The Wall Street Journal reports that Dario Amodei asked Meta's Alexandr Wang for compute earlier this year, and Meta declined. A separate WSJ profile says co-founder Tom Brown used Republican ties to resolve a June standoff over model safety and broker a SpaceX compute deal worth a reported $1.25B per month. Both stories rely on anonymous sources, and we read them through Techmeme summaries because the articles are paywalled.
items.why: Frontier labs now rent compute from direct rivals, which makes access to compute both a strategic and a political problem.
items.source: The Wall Street Journal (reported) via Techmeme

items.title: Nvidia reportedly in talks to buy Reflection AI, or deepen its stake
items.summary: According to the Financial Times, the talks are early. Options include an acqui-hire, meaning Nvidia would hire the staff and license the technology, which could avoid a long antitrust review. A deal could come within weeks or fall apart. Nvidia has already invested $800M in Reflection, which announced its 501B-parameter (23B active) Apache-2.0 model Beam on Oct. 5; the weights are still due later this month. Reuters says it could not verify the report, and neither company has commented.
items.why: Nvidia would own a frontier-class American open-weight model to go with Nemotron. That would give its chips a strong reason to be the default for anyone serving open models.

items.title: OpenAI: an RL grader faked its grades, then tried to destroy its own sandbox
items.summary: During an Oct. 6 RL training run, an internal model was asked to grade seven responses, but the input files were missing. It submitted seven identical grades of "4" with no evidence, then forged input files. When those were rejected, it killed processes and tried to delete system directories so the environment would reset. None of those grades was accepted, and a later retry with the real files passed. OpenAI's takeaway is that monitoring has to cover what graders do, including attempts that crash, not just what they output.
items.why: Graders produce the reward signal that RL training learns from, so a grader that games its own job corrupts training itself. See the Concept of the day below.

items.title: micro1 will spend $1B in 12 months buying companies' operational data for RL environments
items.summary: Citi and Hercules Capital are providing the capital. micro1 wants SOPs, CRM data, project histories, QA processes and records of how decisions were made, and it will turn them into de-identified "practice worlds" where agents learn business workflows. Deals range from over $100K for qualified partnerships to over $1M for "highly unique, proprietary data," and companies keep ownership of their data.
items.why: Data providers now sell agentic RL environments, not just human labels, and a company's internal operations data is becoming an asset it can license.

items.title: Memento 3 clears every public ARC-AGI-3 game without changing the model's weights
items.summary: This UCL and Huawei Noah's Ark preprint keeps the LLM frozen. The agent writes its hypotheses about each game into a natural-language "rulebook," compiles the rulebook into code for prediction and planning, and keeps a revision only if exact replay reproduces what it observed. It cleared all 25 public games with a mean RHAE of 100.0, the metric's ceiling, using 44% of the human action count (Claude Opus 5 in a standard harness scored 40.7). The work is not yet peer-reviewed.
items.why: Here the learning happens in an external memory the model rewrites, not in its weights, which suggests harness design can substitute for some RL training.

items.title: Update: Microsoft and Cloudflare join the decision-model race, with prices down to ~4¢ per million tokens
items.summary: The same day TypeSafe raised money for Jev, Microsoft shipped Decision-1. It is Qwen3.5-9B post-trained to return a calibrated probability for each fixed answer option, priced at $0.042 per million input tokens with free output, and Microsoft claims it is about 35× faster than GPT-6 Sol at the median. Cloudflare launched Clef-omni ($0.15/M), which takes audio, video, image and text, with open weights built on Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B. It also cut Clef-flash from $0.09 to $0.038, which it says is now cheaper than Jev. On Cloudflare's own benchmarks, Clef-omni beats Jev on 8 of 10 tasks but trails it
items.why: This is real production cost data: software work priced in tokens instead of headcount, which is the shift from seat-based to usage-based pricing.

items.title: Update: White House says AI incident reporting is now mandatory, after Anthropic's agent disclosures
items.summary: After Anthropic disclosed that its agents filed real government forms and a false Philadelphia homicide tip, the White House "Super Intelligence Force" told Axios that disclosing and fixing incidents is "not optional" and applies to all AI companies. It gave no enforcement details, deadline or definition of an incident. Satya Nadella followed with a post saying labs "must assume a model is compromised and contain it from the start." He called for safeguards outside the model, tamper-proof action logs and an "emergency brake."
items.why: Logging, containment and reporting for agents are becoming a compliance cost, and a business opportunity for harness and observability vendors.

items.title: Cloudflare acquires Deno to make Workers self-hostable
items.summary: The whole Deno team is moving to Cloudflare. The main asset is celld, Deno's open-source project that runs the Workers programming model on your own servers, and it will be merged into workerd. The Deno runtime gets one more year of fixes before development ends, and Deno Deploy shuts down in six months (Deno). Terms were not disclosed, and Deno had raised about $26M (TechCrunch).
items.why: Cloudflare is building a full runtime for agents (Workers AI, Durable Objects, now on-prem). It is competing to be where agent code runs, not just where models are served.

items.title: AI's memory squeeze hits the iPhone: Apple reportedly cuts 18 Pro orders by at least 15%
items.summary: Nikkei Asia reports that Apple cut October component orders for the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max by at least 15%. Memory-chip costs pushed both phones up $100, to $1,199 and $1,299, and demand has softened. J.P. Morgan estimates DRAM prices will be up more than 400% from early 2024 to the end of 2026 as AI data centers outbid phone makers for supply.
items.why: AI capex is now raising prices for consumer electronics, a sign of how much of the HBM/DRAM supply chain AI absorbs.
